subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It
title: Arjun's Money Mystery
hook: Why does a shopkeeper accept coins and notes? Let's find out!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: curious student who loves the market

characters.name: Dadaji
characters.role: wise grandfather who teaches about money

characters.name: Mrs. Sharma
characters.role: vegetable vendor at the local market

slides.title: Arjun's Money Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun discovers why money works.

image.alt: Arjun's Money Mystery — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: The Market Adventure
slides.storyContext: One Sunday morning, Arjun goes to the market with Dadaji to buy vegetables. Mrs. Sharma, the vegetable vendor, gives them fresh tomatoes and spinach. Arjun gives her some coins and notes. Mrs. Sharma smiles and says, 'This is called money—a magical thing that makes trading easy!' Arjun is curious: Why is money magic? Why can't we just swap things?

image.alt: The Market Adventure — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: What is Money?
slides.storyContext: Dadaji explains: Before money, people traded things directly (barter). Arjun's great-great-grandpa might have traded rice for cloth. But that was very hard! What if the cloth seller didn't want rice?

points.text: Money is something everyone agrees has value and accepts in exchange for goods.
It solves the barter problem—everyone accepts money, so you can trade easily.

slides.inSimpleWords: Money is like a magic ticket—everyone wants it, so you can trade it for anything you need.

image.alt: What is Money? — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: Coins: Small but Mighty
slides.storyContext: Arjun touches the coins in his pocket—a shiny ₹1 coin, two ₹5 coins, and a ₹10 coin. Mrs. Sharma says, 'These coins are made of metal and last a very long time.'

points.text: Coins are round, flat metal money with a value stamped on them.
In India, common coins are ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, and ₹10.
Coins are hard to damage and last for many years.

example.problem: Arjun has 3 coins of ₹5 each. How much money does he have?

slides.inSimpleWords: Coins are small pieces of metal worth different amounts—like ₹5, ₹10—and they stay in good shape for years.

image.alt: Coins: Small but Mighty — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: Notes: Bigger Value, Lighter Weight
slides.storyContext: Dadaji pulls out a ₹100 note from his wallet. Arjun is amazed: 'Wow! This thin paper is worth 100 coins?' Dadaji laughs, 'Yes, and much lighter to carry!'

points.text: Notes are paper money printed by the government (Reserve Bank of India makes them).
Each note has a number (the denomination) and is unique to prevent counterfeiting.

example.problem: Dadaji has one ₹100 note and one ₹50 note. How much does he have altogether?

slides.inSimpleWords: Notes are like colored paper money made by the government—they're lighter than coins but worth much more.

image.alt: Notes: Bigger Value, Lighter Weight — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: Why We Use Money Instead of Barter
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks Dadaji, 'Grandfather, why can't we just trade vegetables for cloth like in the old days?' Dadaji smiles and explains with three real problems.

points.label: Problem 1: Double Coincidence
points.text: In barter, the seller must want EXACTLY what the buyer has. Mrs. Sharma sells vegetables but maybe wants cloth. If the cloth seller wants rice (not vegetables), they can't trade!

points.label: Problem 2: Hard to Divide
points.text: If a cow costs 10 chickens, but you only need to trade 7 chickens—you can't cut a chicken! Money divides easily: ₹100 = 2 × ₹50.

points.label: Problem 3: Hard to Store
points.text: You can't store 100 chickens for a year (they spoil or die). But 100 rupees stay in your pocket forever!

slides.inSimpleWords: Money makes trade fair and simple—anyone will take it, it divides easily, and it doesn't spoil.

image.alt: Why We Use Money Instead of Barter — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: The Two Kinds of Money in Your Pocket
slides.storyContext: At the end of their market trip, Arjun counts his money: coins and notes mixed together. He realizes both are money, but they're different.

points.text: Coins: metal, heavy, good for small amounts, lasts forever.
Notes: paper, light, good for bigger amounts, printed by RBI.
Together, coins + notes = the money you use every day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coins are like small change you feel in your hand; notes are like folded paper money for bigger purchases.

image.alt: The Two Kinds of Money in Your Pocket — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: A Day at the Market (Full Example)
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Dadaji go to buy: 1 kg of tomatoes (₹30), 500g of spinach (₹20), and a loaf of bread (₹40). Dadaji gives Mrs. Sharma two ₹50 notes. How much change should they get?

image.alt: A Day at the Market (Full Example) — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: Your Turn: Money at the Shop
slides.storyContext: You go to the corner shop with ₹100 in your pocket. You buy a notebook for ₹35 and a pencil for ₹15. How much money do you have left?

example.problem: Total spent: ₹35 + ₹15 = ₹50. You started with ₹100. Money left = ?

image.alt: Your Turn: Money at the Shop — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Arjun now understands money! Let's recap.

points.text: Money is something everyone accepts in trade—it solves the barter problem.
Coins are small metal money (₹1, ₹5, ₹10 etc.); notes are paper money (₹10, ₹50, ₹100 etc.).
We use money because it's easy to divide, easy to store, and everyone wants it.
Money makes buying and selling simple and fair for everyone.

slides.inSimpleWords: Money is the tool we use to trade fairly for what we need—coins and notes together make it work.

image.alt: What We Learned — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

subject: Financial Literacy
title: Priya's Shopping Puzzle
hook: Should you buy everything you want, or only what you need? Priya finds out!

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: a thoughtful student learning to spend wisely

characters.name: Mom
characters.role: Priya's mother who teaches smart spending

slides.title: Priya's Shopping Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Priya learns the difference between what she needs and what she just wants.

image.alt: Priya's Shopping Puzzle — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: The Festival Fair
slides.storyContext: During the local Diwali fair, Priya's mom gives her ₹500. Priya's eyes grow wide—there are so many stalls! Toys, clothes, jewelry, sweets, games, books! Her friend Dev is already running toward the toy stall. But Priya's mom says, 'Wait. Before you spend, let's think about what you NEED versus what you WANT.' Priya is confused: doesn't she need everything that looks fun?

image.alt: The Festival Fair — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: What Are Needs?
slides.storyContext: Mom sits with Priya and explains: 'Needs are things your body and life require to be healthy and safe.'

points.text: Food (rice, bread, vegetables, milk) to stay strong.
Clothes to cover your body and stay warm.
A home to sleep and be safe.
School books and pencils to learn.
Medicine when you're sick.

example.problem: Priya needs new school shoes (hers are worn out). This costs ₹400. Is this a need or a want?
example.solution: A NEED—school shoes protect her feet and are required for school.

slides.inSimpleWords: Needs are things you must have to be healthy, safe, and to do your work or go to school.

image.alt: What Are Needs? — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: What Are Wants?
slides.storyContext: Priya points at a beautiful toy robot on a stall. Mom says, 'That's a WANT. Wants are things you desire but don't truly need.'

points.text: Toys and games you enjoy but don't use every day.
Extra clothes because they look nice (beyond what you wear).
Sweets and snacks (beyond basic food for health).
Movies, fun outings, video games.
Jewelry, fancy items, new gadgets.

example.problem: Priya sees a ₹250 toy robot. She already has toys at home. Is this a need or a want?
example.solution: A WANT—it's nice to have but she doesn't need it to be healthy or safe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wants are things that make you happy or entertained but you can live without them.

image.alt: What Are Wants? — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: Needs Come First—Smart Spending Rule #1
slides.storyContext: Mom hands Priya a simple rule: 'Every rupee you have should go to needs FIRST. Only spend on wants with leftover money.' Priya nods—this makes sense!

points.text: Priority 1: Buy what you need for health, safety, and learning.
Priority 2: If money is left after needs, then buy a want (if you really want it).
Priority 3: Save any money that's left (for later surprises or emergencies).

example.problem: Priya has ₹500. She needs new shoes (₹400) and school books (₹50). That's ₹450. She wants a toy (₹150). What should she do?
example.solution: First buy needs: ₹400 + ₹50 = ₹450. Left: ₹50. The toy costs ₹150, so she CAN'T afford the want. Better to save the ₹50 or buy a smaller want.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always buy what you need first, then if there's money left, you can spend on wants.

image.alt: Needs Come First—Smart Spending Rule #1 — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: The Trap of Too Many Wants
slides.storyContext: Priya watches Dev at the fair. He buys a toy (₹120), then a game (₹180), then snacks (₹100). He spent ₹400 on things he wanted! By the end, he's out of money and can't buy the winter jacket he actually needs. Mom says gently, 'That's the trap of wants—they add up fast and eat your money.'

points.text: Wants are unlimited—there's always something new and shiny to buy.
If you spend on every want, you'll run out of money for real needs.
Smart spenders pick ONE want they love, not ten small wants.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wants are tempting and endless—if you buy many small wants, you'll waste money and not have enough for needs.

image.alt: The Trap of Too Many Wants — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: Smart Spending at the Fair
slides.storyContext: Priya decides to be smart. She checks her list: 'I need school shoes (₹400) and new socks (₹50). That's ₹450. I have ₹500 left: ₹50. I could save it, or buy ONE small want like a book (₹40).'

points.text: Make a list of needs BEFORE you go shopping.
Buy needs first—don't get distracted by bright, shiny things.
From leftover money, pick ONE want you really love (not many small wants).
Save the rest for later or emergencies.

slides.inSimpleWords: Make a list, buy needs first, pick one small want if there's money left, and save the rest.

image.alt: Smart Spending at the Fair — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: Priya's Smart Shopping (Full Example)
slides.storyContext: Priya goes to the fair with ₹500. She needs: new shoes (₹400), socks (₹50), and wants to buy a book (₹40). How much money does she save?

image.alt: Priya's Smart Shopping (Full Example) — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: Your Turn: Smart Shopping
slides.storyContext: You have ₹300. You need a new school bag (₹200). You want a pencil box (₹50) and a notebook (₹30). Do you have enough? How much is left after buying needs AND one want? Can you buy everything?

example.problem: Needs: ₹200 (bag). Wants: ₹50 (pencil box) + ₹30 (notebook) = ₹80. Total: ₹200 + ₹80 = ₹280. You have ₹300. Left: ?
example.solution: Yes, you can afford everything! Leftover: ₹300 − ₹280 = ₹20.

image.alt: Your Turn: Smart Shopping — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Priya bought her needs, one small want, and saved money. She felt wise and happy!

points.text: Needs are food, clothes, shelter, school, and medicine—things you must have.
Wants are toys, games, snacks, and fun things you enjoy but can live without.
Smart rule: Buy needs FIRST, then one want if money is left, then SAVE.
Don't fall into the trap of many small wants—they add up and waste money.

slides.inSimpleWords: Be smart about money: needs first, one favorite want second, and save the rest.

image.alt: What We Learned — Needs vs Wants — Smart Spending

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit
title: Karan's Piggy Bank Dream
hook: A little money saved each day becomes a big treasure! Watch Karan's dream come true.

characters.name: Karan
characters.role: a boy who saves coins to buy a bicycle

characters.name: Grandmother
characters.role: Karan's wise grandmother who teaches the power of saving

slides.title: Karan's Piggy Bank Dream
slides.storyContext: Karan learns how small savings grow into big dreams.

image.alt: Karan's Piggy Bank Dream — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: The Dream Bicycle
slides.storyContext: Karan is 10 years old. He loves cycling but his bicycle is old and rusty. One day, he sees his neighbor riding a shiny new bicycle. His heart aches—he wants one too! But when he asks his parents, they say, 'A new bicycle costs ₹5,000. That's a lot of money!' Karan feels sad. Then his grandmother calls him over. 'Karan beta, do you really want that bicycle?' Karan nods. 'Then I will teach you a secret—the magic of saving money.' Karan is curious: How can he get ₹5,000?

image.alt: The Dream Bicycle — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: What Does "Saving" Mean?
slides.storyContext: Grandmother gives Karan a piggy bank (a small clay pig with a slot). 'Every rupee you don't spend, put it here. You're saving!' Karan asks, 'But grandmother, what IS saving?'

points.text: Saving means spending LESS than you earn or receive, and keeping the leftover money.
Money you save grows over time and can buy bigger dreams later.
A piggy bank, a box, or a bank account is a safe place to keep saved money.

example.problem: Karan gets ₹100 pocket money each week. He spends ₹70 on snacks and fun. How much can he save?

slides.inSimpleWords: Saving means keeping money instead of spending it all—like a treasure chest that grows bigger each day.

image.alt: What Does "Saving" Mean? — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Why Save? The Power of Saving
slides.storyContext: Grandmother tells Karan four reasons why saving is powerful. 'Listen carefully,' she says, settling in her chair with a warm cup of chai.

points.label: Reason 1: Big Dreams
points.text: A bicycle costs ₹5,000. You can't buy it with ₹100. But if you save ₹100 each month for 50 months, you have ₹5,000!

points.label: Reason 2: Emergencies
points.text: If your school uniform rips or you fall sick and need medicine, saved money helps without asking your parents every time.

points.label: Reason 3: No Borrowing
points.text: If you save, you don't need to borrow money from others and pay it back with extra cost (interest).

points.label: Reason 4: Freedom & Pride
points.text: Money you save is YOURS. You earned it and kept it. That feels amazing!

slides.inSimpleWords: Saving helps you buy big dreams, handle surprises, stay out of debt, and feel proud of yourself.

image.alt: Why Save? The Power of Saving — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: How Much Should You Save? The Saving Rule
slides.storyContext: Karan asks, 'Grandmother, should I save all my pocket money and spend nothing?' She laughs gently. 'No beta, balance is important. There's a simple rule.'

points.text: A good saving rule for kids is: Save at least 1/3 (one-third) of your pocket money.
Example: If you get ₹300 pocket money, save ₹100 and spend ₹200.
Some people save 1/2 (half) or even more if they have a big goal.
The key: Save something from every rupee you receive—make it a HABIT.

example.problem: Karan gets ₹300 pocket money weekly. If he saves 1/3, how much does he save each week?
example.solution: 1/3 of ₹300 = ₹100 saved per week. He spends ₹200.

slides.inSimpleWords: Save at least 1/3 of every rupee you get—make it a habit, not an accident.

image.alt: How Much Should You Save? The Saving Rule — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Small Savings Add Up—The Magic of Time
slides.storyContext: Karan saves ₹100 every week. After one week, he has ₹100. After two weeks, ₹200. But grandmother shows him something magical—a chart of how his savings grow!

points.text: In just under a year, saving ₹100 weekly gives you almost ₹5,000!
This is the magic: small regular savings + TIME = big money.

example.problem: Karan saves ₹50 every day. After 100 days, how much has he saved?

slides.inSimpleWords: Save a little bit every day or week, and time turns it into a big amount—like magic!

image.alt: Small Savings Add Up—The Magic of Time — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Where to Keep Your Savings?
slides.storyContext: Karan asks, 'Grandmother, is a piggy bank safe? What if someone steals it?' Grandmother nods wisely. 'Good question. There are three places.'

points.label: Option 1: Piggy Bank at Home
points.text: Safe from your own spending! You can see your money grow. Good for kids learning to save.

points.label: Option 2: A Locked Box
points.text: A metal box with a key, hidden safely, where only you (and maybe a parent) can open it.

points.label: Option 3: A Bank Account
points.text: A real bank (like ICICI, SBI, Punjab National Bank) keeps your money safe and gives you interest (extra money!) on your savings.

slides.inSimpleWords: Keep savings in a piggy bank, a locked box, or best of all, a bank account that earns extra money.

image.alt: Where to Keep Your Savings? — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Karan's Year of Saving (Full Example)
slides.storyContext: Karan saves ₹100 every week. After 52 weeks (one year), he counts his piggy bank with his grandmother. How much does he have?

example.problem: ₹100 × 52 weeks = ? (This is the amount saved in one year.)
example.solution: ₹100 × 52 = ₹5,200. Karan now has enough for the ₹5,000 bicycle PLUS ₹200 extra!

image.alt: Karan's Year of Saving (Full Example) — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Your Turn: Savings Plan
slides.storyContext: You want to save ₹2,000 for a new school bag and shoes. You get ₹200 pocket money every month. If you save 1/2 of it each month, how many months until you reach your goal?

example.problem: You get ₹200/month. Save 1/2 = ₹100/month. Goal: ₹2,000. Months needed: ₹2,000 ÷ ₹100 = ?
example.solution: 20 months (about 1.5 years). Every rupee saved gets you closer!

image.alt: Your Turn: Savings Plan — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: One year later, Karan rides his shiny new bicycle. He's so proud! Let's recap the lesson.

points.text: Saving means spending less than you earn and keeping the extra money.
You save for big dreams, emergencies, to avoid debt, and to feel proud.
Save at least 1/3 of your pocket money—make it a regular habit.
Small savings + time = big money. A little bit every day or week becomes a fortune!
Keep savings safe: in a piggy bank, a locked box, or best of all, a bank account.

slides.inSimpleWords: Save money regularly from what you get, and your dreams will come true. Start today!

image.alt: What We Learned — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit
